From samarbeid (“cooperation, collaboration”) + vanske (“difficulty, problem”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “cooperation difficulty”.

Compare Norwegian Nynorsk samarbeidsvanske.

19327.etyen:
Compound of G (“G”) + dur (“major”), literally “G major”.
The first element G (“G”) is the name of the musical note G. The second element dur (“major”) is via German Dur (“major”) from Middle High German bēdūre (“B-natural; hard B”), from Medieval Latin b durum (“hard B”). The adjective is from Latin dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Italic *dūros (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós (“long, far”), from the root *dweh₂- (“far, long”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk G-dur, Danish G-dur, Swedish G-dur, German G-Dur and Finnish G-duuri (“G major”).

1000063.etyen:
Borrowed from English Kenya, from the name of Mount Kenya. The modern form was recorded in the 19th century by the German missionary and explorer Johann Ludwig Krapf as Kenia and Kegnia. The deeper origin of the mountain name is unknown. One proposed explanation derives Krapf's forms from Kamba Kĩ-Nyaa or Kamba Kĩlĩma Kĩinyaa. Another connects the name with Kikuyu Kĩrĩma Kĩrĩnyaga (“mountain of brightness; mountain of whiteness”), referring to the contrasting dark rock and snow of the mountain. The female given name is derived from the country name.
Parallel international adaptations include N

1000831.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Djúpvík (“the deep bay”), from djúpr (“deep”) + vík (“bay, inlet”). The name originally belonged to a farm, first recorded in 1432 as Dyupwiik. Doublet of Djupvik, Dybvik, and Dybevik.

1004415.etyen:
An old Norwegian river name, usually connected with the reconstructed Germanic roots *swark- and *swork- (“to darken, become black”), related to svart (“black”); hence probably originally “the dark one”. A sound-symbolic origin, referring to the sound of flowing water, has also been proposed.
Compare the related Norwegian river names Surka, Sørka, Svarka and Sverka.
First attested in the 1432–1433 indirectly in the compound place name Surkomor, now Svorkmo.

1004927.etyen:
From enke (“widow”) + keiserinne (“empress”), literally “widow empress”. The first element enke (“widow”) is from Old Danish ænkia (“widow”), from Proto-Germanic *ainakjǭ (“widow”), based on *ainagaz (“only, sole”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”). The second element keiserinne (“empress”) consists synchronically of keiser (“emperor”) and -inne (“feminine noun suffix”), and continues Old Norse keisarinna (“empress”). The base keiser (“emperor”) is from Old Norse keisari (“emperor”), ultimately from Latin Caesar; the further origin of the Latin name is uncertain.
